lessonTitle: The Genetic Code and Translation: Ribosomes, tRNA and Point Mutations

blocks.text: In some families a four-nucleotide insertion in the HEXA gene shifts the reading frame and causes the fatal neurodegenerative Tay-Sachs disease, whereas in sickle cell disease one single nucleotide change alters just one amino acid in beta-globin. Why does one kind of mutation scramble the protein and another change a single residue? The answer lies in how the ribosome reads the code three letters at a time.

blocks.markdown: **Translation** is the synthesis of a polypeptide whose amino acid sequence is specified by the nucleotide sequence of an mRNA. The **genetic code** is the set of rules for this decoding. The mRNA is read in groups of three nucleotides called **codons**. Because RNA has four bases, there are $4^3 = 64$ possible codons: **61 sense codons** specify the 20 standard amino acids, and **3 stop codons** (UAA, UAG, UGA) signal the end of translation. The codon **AUG** codes for methionine and also serves as the usual **start codon**.

blocks.title: Properties of the genetic code
blocks.text: The code is a triplet code, read without gaps or overlaps from a fixed start codon (so the reading frame is set by the start codon). It is unambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid. It is degenerate (redundant): most amino acids are specified by more than one codon, usually differing at the third position. It is nearly universal: the same code is used by almost all organisms, with minor exceptions, such as in human mitochondria where UGA codes for tryptophan and AUA for methionine.

blocks.markdown: **Degeneracy and wobble.** The redundancy is mostly at the third codon position: for example GUU, GUC, GUA and GUG all code for valine. The anticodon of a tRNA pairs with the codon in an antiparallel manner, but the pairing at the third codon position is looser, a feature called **wobble**, so one tRNA can recognise several codons. Degeneracy buffers the effect of mutations, since many third-position changes are **silent**. Universality allows human genes to be expressed in bacteria, which is the basis of recombinant protein production.

**The machinery.** **Ribosomes** are ribonucleoprotein complexes made of ribosomal RNA and proteins, with a small and a large subunit: 40S and 60S (together 80S) in eukaryotes, and 30S and 50S (together 70S) in bacteria. The ribosome has three tRNA binding sites: **A (aminoacyl) site**, **P (peptidyl) site** and **E (exit) site**. **Transfer RNAs (tRNAs)** are adapters, each with an **anticodon** that pairs with an mRNA codon and an amino acid attached at its 3' end. Each tRNA is loaded with the correct amino acid by a specific **aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase**, using ATP; this 'charging' step is critical for the fidelity of translation.

**Initiation.** In eukaryotes, the small (40S) ribosomal subunit with initiation factors and the initiator **Met-tRNA** binds to the 5' cap of the mRNA, scans along it until it finds the first AUG in a favourable context (the Kozak sequence), and the large (60S) subunit then joins to form the 80S ribosome with the initiator tRNA in the **P site**. **Elongation** is a repeating cycle: (1) a charged tRNA matching the next codon enters the **A site** (delivered by an elongation factor using GTP); (2) the **peptidyl transferase** activity, which is catalysed by ribosomal RNA of the large subunit (a ribozyme), forms a peptide bond, transferring the growing chain to the amino acid on the A-site tRNA; (3) **translocation**, driven by another elongation factor and GTP, moves the ribosome one codon along the mRNA, shifting the tRNAs to the P and E sites. **Termination** occurs when a stop codon (UAA, UAG, UGA) enters the A site: no tRNA recognises it, instead protein **release factors** bind, the polypeptide is released from the tRNA in the P site, and the ribosome dissociates. Polypeptides are made from the amino (N) terminus to the carboxyl (C) terminus.

blocks.title: Translating an mRNA

steps.text: Find the first AUG reading 5' to 3': G C **AUG** GAA UUC AAA UAA GC. The reading frame starts at AUG.
Split into codons from AUG: AUG, GAA, UUC, AAA, UAA.
Look up each codon: AUG = Met, GAA = Glu, UUC = Phe, AAA = Lys, UAA = stop.

blocks.answer: The peptide is Met-Glu-Phe-Lys (N terminus to C terminus); UAA stops translation, and the nucleotides after it are not translated.

blocks.markdown: **Point mutations and their effects.** A **point mutation** is a change in a single nucleotide. Those that substitute one base for another are: **silent** (the new codon codes for the same amino acid, often at the third position, with no change in protein); **missense** (the new codon codes for a different amino acid; the effect depends on how different the new residue is and where in the protein it lies); and **nonsense** (the new codon is a stop codon, giving a truncated protein, which is often degraded and the mRNA may be destroyed by nonsense-mediated decay). A **frameshift** results from the insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides that is **not a multiple of three**; the reading frame shifts and all downstream codons are changed, usually creating a premature stop codon, so the protein is usually nonfunctional. Insertion or deletion of a multiple of three nucleotides keeps the frame (in-frame), adding or removing amino acids.

blocks.title: Classifying mutations in a short coding sequence
blocks.prompt: The normal mRNA reads 5'-AUG GAA UUC AAA UAA-3' (Met-Glu-Phe-Lys-stop). Classify each mutation: (a) UUC to UUU; (b) GAA to UAA; (c) AAA to AAC; (d) insertion of a G after AUG.

steps.text: (a) UUU also codes for Phe, so the protein is unchanged: silent.
(b) UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends after Met: nonsense (the peptide is just Met).
(c) AAC codes for Asn instead of Lys: missense.
(d) Inserting one nucleotide shifts the frame: AUG GGA AUU CAA AUA A.. now reads Met-Gly-Ile-Gln-Ile... so every downstream amino acid is changed: frameshift.

blocks.title: Why antibiotics can target bacterial translation
blocks.text: Bacterial ribosomes (70S) differ from human cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S). Several antibiotics exploit this: for example tetracyclines block binding of aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site, chloramphenicol inhibits peptidyl transferase in the 50S subunit, and aminoglycosides cause misreading of the code (pharmacology teaching examples).

items: 64 codons: 61 sense, 3 stop; AUG is start; the code is degenerate, unambiguous and almost universal.
Initiation, elongation (A site entry, peptide bond, translocation) and termination (release factors at stop codons).
Silent, missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations have different consequences.
Frameshifts arise from insertions or deletions not divisible by three.

blocks.title: Frameshift check
blocks.text: To decide whether an insertion or deletion causes a frameshift, check whether the number of nucleotides is divisible by three; if so, it is in-frame and only adds or removes whole amino acids.

points: The genetic code is read in triplet codons: 61 sense codons and 3 stop codons; it is degenerate (mostly at the third position), unambiguous and almost universal.
Translation uses ribosomes, charged tRNAs and the A, P and E sites; it proceeds by initiation at AUG, cycles of elongation and termination at a stop codon with release factors.
Point mutations are silent, missense or nonsense; insertions or deletions not divisible by three cause frameshifts.

questions.stem: The codons GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine. Which property of the genetic code does this illustrate?

options.text: Degeneracy (redundancy)
Universality
Ambiguity
Overlapping

distractorRationale.a: Correct: several codons specify the same amino acid.
distractorRationale.b: Universality refers to the same code being used across organisms.
distractorRationale.c: The code is unambiguous: each codon specifies only one amino acid.

questions.explanation: Degeneracy means that more than one codon can code for the same amino acid, with variation mostly at the third position. Because each codon still specifies only one amino acid, the code remains unambiguous.

questions.stem: A human gene is inserted into bacteria and the bacteria produce the correct human protein. Which property of the code makes this possible?

options.text: The code is almost universal across organisms
The code is degenerate
Bacteria have an 80S ribosome like humans
Human mRNA is translated in bacterial mitochondria

questions.correctOptionText: The code is almost universal across organisms

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the same codons specify the same amino acids in humans and bacteria.
distractorRationale.b: Degeneracy does not make codons interchangeable between organisms.

questions.explanation: Almost all organisms use the same codon-amino acid assignments, so the bacterial ribosome decodes a human mRNA correctly. Differences in the ribosome (70S versus 80S) do not alter the code.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes elongation of the polypeptide chain?

options.text: A charged tRNA enters the A site, a peptide bond is formed by peptidyl transferase, and the ribosome translocates by one codon
A release factor enters the A site and joins the next amino acid
The small subunit scans the mRNA and the large subunit adds amino acids
The tRNA in the P site leaves and the A site is left empty for the stop codon

questions.correctOptionText: A charged tRNA enters the A site, a peptide bond is formed by peptidyl transferase, and the ribosome translocates by one codon

distractorRationale.b: Release factors act at termination, not elongation.

questions.explanation: Elongation cycles through aminoacyl-tRNA delivery to the A site, peptide bond formation catalysed by the rRNA of the large subunit, and translocation by one codon. Release factors act only at stop codons.

questions.stem: What happens when a stop codon enters the A site of the ribosome?

options.text: Release factors bind and the completed polypeptide is released
A tRNA with an anticodon complementary to the stop codon enters
The ribosome shifts the reading frame and continues
Methionine is added as the last amino acid

questions.correctOptionText: Release factors bind and the completed polypeptide is released

distractorRationale.a: Correct: release factors recognise stop codons and trigger hydrolysis of the peptide-tRNA bond.
distractorRationale.b: No normal tRNA recognises stop codons.
distractorRationale.c: Frame shifting is not part of normal termination.
distractorRationale.d: Methionine is the start amino acid, not added at termination.

questions.explanation: Stop codons are not recognised by tRNAs; they are recognised by release factors, which cause hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the tRNA in the P site. The ribosome then dissociates.

questions.stem: The normal mRNA reads 5'-AUG CCU AAG GAU CGU UGA-3' (Met-Pro-Lys-Asp-Arg-stop). A mutation changes AAG to UAG. How should this be classified and what is the likely effect?

options.text: Nonsense mutation; truncated protein of two amino acids
Missense mutation; Lys replaced by another amino acid
Silent mutation; no change
Frameshift mutation; all downstream amino acids altered

questions.correctOptionText: Nonsense mutation; truncated protein of two amino acids

distractorRationale.a: Correct: UAG is a stop codon, so only Met-Pro is made.
distractorRationale.b: UAG does not code for an amino acid.
distractorRationale.c: The change creates a stop codon, so the protein is altered.
distractorRationale.d: A substitution keeps the reading frame; there is no insertion or deletion.

questions.explanation: UAG is a stop codon, so translation terminates after codon 2 (Met-Pro), giving a truncated product. Because a single base is substituted and the frame is unchanged, it is a nonsense mutation rather than a frameshift.

questions.stem: The coding region of an mRNA, from the AUG start codon to the end of the stop codon, is 1,305 nucleotides long. A nonsense mutation converts codon 120 (counting the start codon AUG as codon 1) to a stop codon. What percentage of the full-length protein, as a number of amino acids, is made as the truncated polypeptide? Give your answer to the nearest whole percent (%).
questions.explanation: 1,305 nucleotides is 435 codons, of which the last is the stop codon, so the full-length protein has 434 amino acids. A stop at codon 120 leaves codons 1-119, which is 119 amino acids. The fraction retained is 119/434 = 0.274, or about 27%.

questions.stem: True or false: A deletion of three consecutive nucleotides within the coding region always causes a frameshift.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A deletion of a multiple of three nucleotides keeps the reading frame (in-frame), removing one or more amino acids but leaving downstream codons unchanged. Frameshifts require insertions or deletions not divisible by three.

questions.stem: Describe the properties of the genetic code and explain what is meant by wobble, giving one consequence of degeneracy for the effect of mutations.
markingGuide: Triplet code: 64 codons, 61 sense and 3 stop (UAA, UAG, UGA); AUG is start and codes for methionine.
Degenerate: most amino acids have more than one codon, differing mainly at the third position.
Unambiguous: each codon specifies one amino acid; non-overlapping and read from a fixed start.
Nearly universal, with exceptions such as human mitochondria.
Wobble: looser base pairing at the third codon position, so one tRNA can read several codons.
Consequence: third-position changes are often silent, so many mutations do not alter the protein.
questions.explanation: The code's degeneracy means that many substitutions are tolerated without changing the amino acid, and wobble lets a limited set of tRNAs read all codons.

questions.stem: Outline the three stages of translation in eukaryotes, stating the role of the A, P and E sites, charged tRNA, peptidyl transferase and release factors.
markingGuide: Initiation: 40S subunit with initiation factors and Met-tRNA binds the 5' cap, scans to the first AUG; 60S subunit joins; initiator tRNA in the P site.
Charging: aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach the correct amino acid to its tRNA using ATP.

Elongation: charged tRNA enters the A site; peptidyl transferase (rRNA of the large subunit) forms the peptide bond; translocation (GTP-dependent) moves tRNAs to P and E sites and the ribosome one codon along.
Termination: stop codon in the A site is recognised by release factors, which release the polypeptide; the ribosome dissociates.
Synthesis proceeds from N-terminus to C-terminus as mRNA is read 5' to 3'.
questions.explanation: Translation proceeds through assembly at the start codon, repeated cycles of codon matching, bond formation and translocation, and release at a stop codon.

questions.stem: The normal mRNA reads 5'-AUG CCU AAG GAU CGU UGA-3'. Classify each of the following changes and predict the effect on the polypeptide: (a) CCU to CCC; (b) GAU to GAG; (c) insertion of a single nucleotide between AAG and GAU.
markingGuide: (a) CCC also codes for Pro: silent mutation; no change in the protein.
(b) GAG codes for Glu instead of Asp: missense mutation (conservative, both acidic), so the protein may be unaffected or mildly affected.

(c) Insertion of one nucleotide (not a multiple of three): frameshift; codons downstream are read in a different frame, so all later amino acids change and the stop codon is typically lost or a premature stop appears, usually producing a nonfunctional protein.
Correct definitions used for each class.
questions.explanation: Silent changes retain the amino acid, missense changes substitute a different one and frameshifts alter the reading frame downstream, usually with the most severe consequences.
